summary: Only about 1,510 people live in Irwindale, yet the city sprawls across 9.6 square miles — a density of just 157 residents per square mile — because the vast majority of its land is given over to rock quarries, ready-mix concrete plants, and industrial operations that have supplied construction materials across the Los Angeles Basin for decades. The Miller Brewing facility (now operated under Molson Coors) and Sriracha producer Huy Fong Foods both operate here, making Irwindale one of those rare tiny cities that punches absurdly above its weight as a job center; the daytime working population dwarfs the residential count. The San Gabriel Mountains rise immediately to the north, and the flat valley floor is carved up by the San Gabriel River channel and laced with freight rail, giving the landscape a rugged, utilitarian texture interrupted by pockets of modest residential streets. A median household income of $113,250 against a median home value near $645,800 yields a price-to-income ratio around 5.7 — tight but not crushing by LA County standards — though the housing stock itself is extremely limited. Property crime rates are strikingly high per capita (over 15,000 per 100K), but that figure is inflated by a denominator of fewer than two thousand residents spread across a landscape dominated by commercial and industrial parcels. With 9.2 hours of daily sunshine and average highs around 78°F, the climate is classic inland San Gabriel Valley — warm, dry, and unshaded. Irwindale is less a place people move *to* than a place that exists in fascinating tension between an enormous industrial footprint and a tiny residential population sheltered at its edges.
